items.explanation: The treaty was a settlement between two rival Catholic powers competing for the same newly encountered lands. With the Reconquista completed in 1492, Spain and Portugal both sought overseas empires, and the pope acted as mediator because both crowns recognized papal authority over such divisions.
items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms (Treaty of Tordesillas) — agreement dividing non-European lands between Spain and Portugal

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Reformation began in 1517, more than two decades after the treaty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because Ottoman control of eastern trade routes motivated Portugal's search for a sea route to Asia, but the treaty itself was about dividing claims between Spain and Portugal, not about the Ottomans.
option_explanations.C: Right because the treaty directly reflects papal mediation of imperial rivalry between the two Catholic Iberian crowns.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because organized European debate over Indigenous rights, such as the Valladolid debate, came decades later in the 1550s.

options: (A) The Protestant Reformation's division of Europe into rival churches
(B) The Ottoman Empire's closure of overland trade routes to Asia, which pushed European powers to seek wealth through new overseas ventures
(C) Papal mediation of the imperial rivalry between Catholic Spain and Portugal over newly encountered lands
(D) Growing European concern about the rights of Indigenous peoples in the Americas
items.stem: In 1494 Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, which drew a line through the Atlantic assigning newly encountered lands west of the line to Spain and east of it to Portugal. Which broader historical development best explains the context in which this treaty was made?

stimulus.text: The 1494 agreement, brokered with the pope's approval, divided all newly discovered lands between the two Iberian crowns along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.

items.explanation: The debate drew on the scholastic natural-law tradition and classical authorities like Aristotle to argue about just war and the rights of peoples encountered through empire. It belongs to a sixteenth-century European intellectual context in which conquest itself was contested, not to later rights movements.
items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms (Valladolid Debate) — formal dispute between Las Casas and Sepulveda over the rights and rational humanity of Native peoples

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Enlightenment is an eighteenth-century development, two centuries after Valladolid.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the debate was an internal Catholic dispute about the legitimacy of conquest, not a Protestant attack on the Church.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Spanish Empire was at the height of its wealth in this era, with silver flowing from the Americas.
option_explanations.D: Right because the debaters argued from natural law and just-war theory, the sixteenth-century framework for judging conquest.

options: (A) The spread of Enlightenment ideas about universal human rights
(B) Protestant reformers' attacks on the Spanish Catholic Church and its claims to authority in the Americas
(C) The economic collapse of the Spanish Empire in the late sixteenth century
(D) Sixteenth-century European arguments over natural law and just war
items.stem: In 1550-1551, the Dominican friar Bartolome de las Casas and the scholar Juan Gines de Sepulveda formally debated before a Spanish council whether Native peoples of the Americas possessed natural rights and rational humanity. Which broader development best explains why this debate took place when and where it did?

stimulus.text: The Valladolid debate of 1550-1551: Las Casas argued that Native peoples had natural rights and should not be enslaved; Sepulveda, drawing on Aristotle, argued they were naturally inferior and that conquest was just.

items.explanation: Columbus sailed seeking Asia, but accounts such as Vespucci's suggested a 'new world.' Waldseemuller acted on that emerging understanding by giving the new continents a distinct name, marking Europe's gradual recognition that these lands were not part of Asia.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Columbus was hunting for Asia across four voyages; a German cartographer labeled the new continent 'America' in 1507

option_explanations.A: Right because the 'America' label records the moment European geography absorbed the idea of a fourth, previously unknown continent.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the conquests of the Mexica (1519-1521) and Inca (1532) happened after 1507.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Reformation began in 1517, a decade after this map.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because Portuguese African trading posts were part of the search for an Asian sea route, not the naming of the American continents.

options: (A) Europe's growing realization that Columbus had reached a new continent, not Asia
(B) Spain's completion of its conquest of the Mexica and Inca empires
(C) The Protestant Reformation's challenge to Catholic authority over geography and exploration
(D) Portugal's establishment of trading posts along the African coast
items.stem: This 1507 map by the German cartographer Martin Waldseemuller was the first to label the western continents 'America.' Which broader development best explains the context in which this map was produced?

stimulus.image_caption: Detail of Martin Waldseemuller's 1507 world map, the first to use the name 'America' for the western continents.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1507 printed map; pre-1930, public domain per Commons license tag

items.explanation: American silver gave Spain the revenues to fund armies, navies, and state-building during an era of intense European rivalry. The long-run significance of Potosi is that New World bullion underwrote European state power.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — silver, above all the great mines at Potosi (1545), whose output flowed into European treasuries and the world economy; §What the exam tests here — American silver financed European state power

option_explanations.A: Wrong because silver was used to buy Asian goods; it deepened rather than ended Europe's trade with Asia.
option_explanations.B: Right because Potosi's output flowed into treasuries that financed the military competition among European states.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the encomienda was curbed by the New Laws of 1542 for moral and political reasons, unrelated to silver revenues.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because Andean Native populations collapsed from disease and mining labor, rather than recovering.

options: (A) It ended European dependence on Asian trade goods
(B) It financed the military and state power of competing European crowns
(C) It allowed Spain to abolish the encomienda system
(D) It drew thousands of European migrants to the Andes, transforming the region's colonial cities and labor markets
items.stem: After 1545, the silver mines at Potosi in the Andes produced enormous wealth that flowed into Spanish treasuries and across the world economy. Which broader development best explains the historical significance of Potosi's silver?

stimulus.text: The mines at Potosi, opened in 1545, became the richest silver source in the Spanish Empire; their output flowed into European treasuries and the wider world economy.

items.explanation: These engravings fed the 'Black Legend' — the image of Spanish cruelty spread by Spain's rivals. Dutch and English publishers circulated Las Casas's accounts with lurid illustrations to discredit Spain while competing with it for empire.
items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms (Black Legend) — the image of Spanish cruelty in the Americas, spread by Spain's rivals

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Spanish crown had no interest in advertising its own cruelty; the images were published by its rivals.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the engravings appeared in Protestant northern European editions aimed at discrediting Spain, not in missionary recruitment.
option_explanations.C: Right because the Black Legend was spread by Spain's imperial rivals as propaganda in their competition with Spain.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because there were no such appeals; the images were produced by Europeans for European audiences.

options: (A) The Spanish crown's campaign to publicize its own colonial reforms
(B) Catholic missionaries' efforts to recruit new clergy and funding for the American missions
(C) Rival European powers' use of anti-Spanish propaganda amid imperial competition
(D) Native American leaders' appeals for European military aid
items.stem: Images like this one, depicting Spanish cruelty toward Native peoples, circulated widely in northern Europe in the 1500s and 1600s. Which broader development best explains their circulation?

stimulus.image_caption: Engraving from a 1665 German edition of Bartolome de las Casas's writings, depicting Spanish cruelty toward Native peoples in the Americas.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1665 engraving; pre-1930, public domain per Commons license tag

items.explanation: The catastrophe was biological: smallpox, measles, and influenza struck populations with no prior exposure and no immunity. These virgin-soil epidemics killed enormous numbers, which in turn made Spanish conquest easier and created the labor shortage that drove the shift to African slavery.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — epidemic disease, which killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity; Columbian Exchange brought smallpox, measles, influenza causing demographic catastrophe

option_explanations.A: Wrong because livestock altered landscapes and diets, but they did not cause the population collapse.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because there was no such mass migration; populations collapsed in place.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Spanish crown sought Native labor and tribute, not extermination; the catastrophe came from disease rather than policy.
option_explanations.D: Right because Old World diseases devastated Native populations lacking immunity, the central demographic fact of the Columbian Exchange.

options: (A) The introduction of European livestock, which trampled Native fields and disrupted established food supplies
(B) Mass migration of Native peoples to French trading posts
(C) The Spanish crown's official policy of extermination
(D) The spread of Old World diseases like smallpox to populations with no immunity
items.stem: Within a century of sustained contact, Native populations in many parts of the Spanish colonies had collapsed catastrophically. Which broader process best explains the context of this demographic catastrophe?

stimulus.text: Spanish accounts from the 1500s describe whole villages emptied by sickness within weeks of contact, long before most Native peoples ever saw a Spanish soldier.

items.explanation: The review stresses that agriculture was the great divide: where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed. Cahokia's scale is evidence of that pattern — Three Sisters agriculture (maize, beans, squash) sustaining a large, stratified Mississippian society.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Cahokia held tens of thousands around 1100; the single biggest divide was agriculture: where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed; §Key terms (Three Sisters agriculture)

option_explanations.A: Right because maize-based farming could feed dense, settled populations, which in turn supported Cahokia's size and mound-building hierarchy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because Cahokia reached its height around 1100, centuries before any Spanish contact.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because horses arrived with Europeans after 1492, long after Cahokia's peak.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Inca road system never extended into North America.

options: (A) Maize-based agriculture supporting dense, settled populations and complex hierarchies
(B) Trade with Spanish explorers in the 1500s
(C) The adoption of horses from European colonists
(D) The spread of the Inca Empire's road and storehouse system northward into North America
items.stem: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, held tens of thousands of residents around 1100, with massive earthen mounds. Which broader development best explains how a society of this scale arose in the North American interior?

stimulus.image_caption: Illustration of the earthen mounds at Cahokia, the largest Mississippian center north of Mexico.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Illustration from a pre-1930 publication; public domain per Commons license tag

items.explanation: The French economic base was furs, and furs required Native hunters and trappers. Conquest and large-scale settler displacement would have destroyed the very labor force the trade depended on, so alliance served French interests better — the opposite incentive from Spain's mining and plantation economy.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — French built an empire on fur trade and Native alliances rather than mines and missions; §What the exam tests here — compare the three European models

option_explanations.A: Wrong because France possessed capable ocean-going ships; technology did not prevent French conquest elsewhere.
option_explanations.B: Right because the fur trade's dependence on Native hunters made cooperation more profitable than conquest.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the French also used coercion; no such blanket legal prohibition shaped their colonial model.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because France lacked major silver colonies; the fur trade was its American economic base.

options: (A) France lacked the naval technology needed for transatlantic conquest
(B) The fur trade depended on Native hunters, so cooperation served French interests better than conquest
(C) French royal decrees strictly forbidding the enslavement or coercion of Native peoples anywhere in the North American colonies
(D) France had already secured enough silver from its other colonies
items.stem: Unlike Spain, France built its North American presence around the fur trade and alliances with Native peoples rather than mines, missions, and large settler populations. Which of the following best evaluates this difference?

stimulus.text: French traders and Jesuits ranged inland from Quebec (founded 1608), building partnerships with Native nations while the French settler population stayed small.

items.explanation: The Reconquista ended in 1492 with the fall of Granada, leaving Spain with a crusading military culture and an appetite for conquest. That ethos — conquest framed as Christian mission — carried directly into the conquistadors' campaigns in the Americas.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — The Reconquista ended in 1492 when Granada fell, leaving Spain with a crusading military culture and a taste for conquest

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Hundred Years' War was an Anglo-French conflict with no bearing on Spanish colonial methods.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the Reformation began in 1517, after the conquest ethos was already formed.
option_explanations.C: Right because the centuries of religious warfare in Iberia shaped Spain's crusading approach to the Americas.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the 1453 fall of Constantinople affected eastern Mediterranean trade, not Spanish conquest culture.

options: (A) The Hundred Years' War between England and France and its chivalric military culture
(B) The Protestant Reformation
(C) The Reconquista, completed in 1492, which shaped Spain's crusading culture
(D) The fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks
items.stem: Spain's approach to the Americas — military conquest justified as a Christian crusade — is best understood in the context of which earlier development?

stimulus.text: Spanish conquistadors described their campaigns in the language of holy war, seeking gold, glory, and royal favor in the name of the Catholic faith.

items.explanation: England spent the late 1500s consumed by religious turmoil at home and expensive conflict with Spain. Only after the Armada's defeat in 1588 weakened Spain could England turn seriously to sustained colonization, with Jamestown following in 1607.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — England tried and failed at Roanoke in 1587, then benefited from Spain's weakening after the Armada's defeat in 1588; by 1607 Jamestown was founded

option_explanations.A: Right because domestic religious conflict and the war with Spain delayed England's colonial efforts until Spain's naval power broke.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because England actively sought overseas trade and plunder throughout the 1500s through privateers and early ventures.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because no such papal decree existed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because England and France were rivals, not allies, in this era.

options: (A) Religious turmoil at home and a costly war with Spain that delayed English colonization
(B) England's lack of interest in overseas trade and colonization until well into the 1700s
(C) A papal decree forbidding Protestant nations from planting colonies anywhere in the Americas
(D) The English crown's long-standing military alliance with France against Spanish power
items.stem: England's first attempt at a permanent American colony, Roanoke (1587), failed, and sustained English colonization did not begin until Jamestown in 1607 — more than a century after Columbus. Which broader development best explains England's late start?

stimulus.text: Roanoke's colonists vanished in the late 1580s; nearly twenty years passed before England planted another colony at Jamestown.
